However, syllables which are assigned H or HL from any of the tonal melodies H, HL, or LHL are more prominent that syllables which are assigned L. new_statements.rule_in_words: Mian is a word-tone language (melodies L, H, LH, LHL, HL assigned to the word); each stem also carries a lexical 'accent' that anchors the melody, regularly on the last stem syllable (on the first syllable of nominals whose first nucleus is pharyngealized /a/; verbs are unaccented, stem-accented or off-stem-accented). There is no independent, consistent word stress: perceived prominence (greater length, high or falling pitch) simply falls on whichever syllables receive H or HL. Smith & Weston 1974:25 concur for the same (eastern) variety: stress non-contrastive, carried by the high/high-falling-toned syllable, otherwise syllables equally stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; Smith & Weston 1974:25 say multiple high-toned syllables 'receive equal stress' and all-low words have equal stress on every syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent on the initial syllable in a few nominals with pharyngealized /a/ in the first syllable (kaˤwá 'steel axe', ǎalá 'lie'); off-stem-accented verbs shift the accent one syllable right when suffixed; inherently accented Future/irrealis suffixes -amab/-omab; H tone on subject marker in non-hodiernal past.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (stem plus suffixes/clitics form one tonal domain; article =e/=i included in noun tone domain). CAVEAT: all of this is stated for the EASTern dialect (mian1256); Fedden treats Suganga/Wagarabai as the western dialect of the same language but gives no West-Mian prosodic data.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog's Suganga (suga1249, [sug]; alt. Wagarabai, North Mianmin, Blimo) is what Fedden calls the West Mian(min) dialect, spoken around Yapsiei (~1,000 speakers): 'West Mianmin (also known as Wagarabai or Suganga)' (Fedden 2007: 20). Every prosodic statement located -- Fedden 2006/2007/2011 (villages around Mianmin airstrip) and Smith & Weston 1974 (Sokabib) -- describes EAST Mian = Glottolog mian1256 [mpt], which is a separate target key. Fedden states explicitly that his description 'is based on the eastern dialect' (p. 28). No source gives first-hand phonological data for Suganga/West Mian beyond Healey's 240-word lists; the quoted statement therefore applies to suga1249 only by Fedden's same-language claim, and should be catalogued under mian1256, with suga1249 cross-referenced rather than counted separately.

sources.note: Describes EAST Mian; names West Mianmin = Wagarabai = Suganga (Yapsiei, ~1,000 speakers) as the other dialect (p. 20) and says the description 'is based on the eastern dialect' (p. 28). Word-tone language: every stem has one tonal melody (L, H, LH, LHL, HL) plus a lexical 'accent' (anchor for the melody) regularly on the last stem syllable, initial if that syllable has pharyngealized /a/ (2.5.3 p. 57, 2.8.2 p. 70); 2.8.10 p. 98: 'There are no consistent stress patterns in Mian'; H/HL-toned syllables are more prominent (longer, high/falling pitch).

sources.note: Earlier analysis (East Mian): 'Stress and tone are distinct phenomena. The domain of stress in Mian is the word. Stress regularly falls on the final syllable in nouns, but can fall on the first syllable in disyllabic nouns if this syllable contains a pharyngealized /a/' (PDF p. 4); tone melody anchors to the stressed syllable. Recast as lexical 'accent' in the 2007/2011 grammar.

sources.note: East Mian (data from Sokabib). Sec. 4.3.2 p. 25: 'Stress is non-contrastive in the Mianmin language. If there is only one high tone or high falling in the word, it will take the stress. Should there be more than one high tone or high glide they will receive equal stress. If all syllables in a word are low tone or low rising each syllable receives equal stress.' Four tonemes.
